findings.title: Google token refresh stores the Zod wrapper as the credential
findings.body: After refreshing, Google CalendarService passes the updated credential object to parseRefreshTokenResponse and writes the return value directly to credential.key. That helper returns the Zod safeParse result {success: true, data: {...}}, not the token object (Office 365 and Zoom read .data). The next GoogleCalendarService constructor runs googleCredentialSchema.parse on that wrapper, which no longer has access_token at the top level, and throws. This runs whenever the access token is expiring, including when credential sync is disabled, so existing Google Calendar connections break until the user reconnects. If the Prisma write throws, the catch treats any error other than invalid_grant as recoverable and returns the old client, so the new token is never stored either.

findings.title: Missing refresh_token is overwritten with the literal "refresh_token"
findings.body: After a successful parse, if refresh_token is missing the helper sets data.refresh_token to the string "refresh_token". This runs for the normal provider schema and the sync schema. Office 365 calendar then spreads tokenResponse.data onto the stored credential and writes it (office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts around line 264). Microsoft often omits refresh_token on refresh and expects the previous one to be kept; the Office 365 schema marks it optional for that reason. The next refresh sends grant refresh_token=refresh_token, Microsoft returns invalid_grant, and the connection stays dead until the user reconnects. In sync mode the minimum schema strips the real refresh_token first, so this always fires, and Zoom then saves that literal (zoomvideo/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts line 120) in place of the real refresh token.

findings.title: Salesforce refresh calls prisma without importing it
findings.body: The new getClient path calls prisma.credential.update after exchanging the refresh token, but this file never imports prisma. Reaching that line throws ReferenceError: prisma is not defined and fails typecheck. getClient runs from the SalesforceCalendarService constructor, so every Salesforce create, update, or availability check throws and no connection is returned. This is not gated on credential sync, so it breaks existing Salesforce installs on deploy.

findings.title: Sync token schema drops every field except access_token
findings.body: minimumTokenResponseSchema is used whenever credential sync and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set. The computed keys z.string().toString() and z.string().optional().toString() are not Zod wildcards; both become "[object Object]", so the second overwrites the first. The schema only requires access_token and z.object strips unknown keys by default (there is no passthrough). Expiry, refresh_token, scope, and instance_url are discarded. Office 365, Zoom, and Salesforce then persist that stripped object. Zoom also sets expiry_date from the missing expires_in, which becomes NaN. A sync refresh therefore corrupts the stored credential instead of updating it.

findings.title: Sync refresh returns a fetch Response callers cannot read
findings.body: When credential sync is on, refreshOAuthTokens returns the raw fetch Response and never checks response.ok or parses JSON. Callers still expect the old provider return value. Google CalendarService reads res.data, which exists on the Gaxios result and not on a fetch Response, so token.access_token throws; the catch ignores anything other than invalid_grant and the access token is never updated. HubSpot treats the Response as a HubspotToken and reads camelCase accessToken/expiresIn. Zoho Bigin and Zoho CRM read axios response.data and throw or skip the update. Webex still validates with webexRefreshedTokenSchema, which requires a fixed scope, token_type "Bearer", refresh_token, and refresh_token_expires_in, so the documented access-token-and-expiry payload is always rejected. Office 365 video replaces the whole credential key with the parsed body and drops refresh_token and email if they are absent. Enabling CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT therefore breaks refresh for the apps this PR wires up.

findings.title: Salesforce client keeps the pre-refresh access token
findings.body: After a successful token response, getClient saves accessTokenParsed.data.access_token but returns a jsforce Connection still configured with credentialKey.access_token and credentialKey.instance_url from before the refresh. If the stored access token is already expired, the API call that triggered getClient uses that expired token and can 401 even though a fresh token was just fetched. The new token is only used on a later request, and only if the database update succeeded.

findings.title: Zoho Bigin sends the credential id as calcomUserId
findings.body: refreshAccessToken passes credentialId, which is credential.id, as the third argument to refreshOAuthTokens. That argument is the Cal.com user id and is sent as calcomUserId. With sync enabled, the parent looks up tokens by a credential primary key, not the user, and can return another user's tokens when a user id collides with this credential id. The following code expects an axios response and reads tokenInfo.data; a fetch Response has no data, so it throws before the local update today. Fixing response parsing without fixing this argument would then write the other user's Zoho tokens onto this credential. Other adapters pass credential.userId.

findings.title: Salesforce refresh fails unless statusText is exactly "OK"
findings.body: The new token request throws HttpError when response.statusText is not the string "OK", before reading the body. Node fetch/undici often leaves statusText empty, especially on HTTP/2, which login.salesforce.com supports. A 200 with an empty or different reason phrase is treated as failure, getClient never returns a connection, and Salesforce calendar operations fail. The check should use response.ok or response.status.

findings.title: Salesforce refreshes the OAuth token on every client construction
findings.body: getClient always POSTs to the Salesforce token endpoint before building the connection, with no check that the stored access token is still valid. Availability and booking construct SalesforceCalendarService often, so each call adds a token round trip and consumes Salesforce OAuth quota. Previously the connection was created from the stored token and jsforce refreshed only when Salesforce rejected it. This extra call is not limited to credential sync, so it regresses every Salesforce user, and a token-endpoint failure now breaks operations that still had a valid access token.

findings.title: Outbound credential sync request is unauthenticated
findings.body: The POST to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT sends only calcomUserId and appSlug. It does not send CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET, a signature, or an Authorization header, and it does not check response.ok. The inbound webhook that writes credentials requires the shared secret, but the call that returns live access tokens does not prove it came from this Cal.com instance. An endpoint implemented to match this client cannot tell Cal.com from any other caller, so anyone who can reach that URL can request access tokens for arbitrary user ids and app slugs.

findings.title: Credential webhook can insert duplicate rows
findings.body: The handler uses findFirst and then updates or creates, with no transaction, lock, or unique constraint on (userId, appId). userId and type are not unique on Credential (other OAuth callbacks already special-case duplicates). Two deliveries for the same user and app, including a retry, can both see no row and both insert. findFirst has no orderBy, so a later sync updates an arbitrary duplicate while calendar code that also uses findFirst can keep the stale key. The user ends up with two credentials and the integration may keep using outdated tokens.

findings.title: Credential sync does not clear the invalid flag
findings.body: The update path writes only key and does not set invalid to false. Google, Webex, and Zoom set invalid after invalid_grant and then skip that credential. If a self-hoster pushes a fresh key for that user, this endpoint still returns 200, but Cal.com keeps ignoring the row, so the integration stays disconnected until the flag is cleared or the user reinstalls the app.

findings.title: Webhook turns bad bodies and ciphertext into unhandled 500s
findings.body: appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse throws a ZodError on a missing or wrong-typed body, and JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...)) throws if the ciphertext, key, or plaintext is invalid. Nothing catches those errors, and the handler does not require POST. The parent sync client gets a 500 instead of 400, cannot tell a bad payload from an outage, and may retry indefinitely. A decrypt exception can also leak crypto library details in the error response.

findings.title: Zoom sync slug is "zoomvideo" but credentials are stored as "zoom"
findings.body: refreshOAuthTokens is called with appSlug "zoomvideo", but the Zoom callback creates the credential with appId "zoom", and the new webhook stores appId from the app metadata slug, which is "zoom" for this app. The parent platform is the source of truth keyed by slug. A sync or refresh using one of these strings will not find the credential written under the other, so Zoom tokens will not update, or a second credential will be created under the wrong slug and never used by the video adapter.

findings.title: Lark deletes the credential before sync refresh can run
findings.body: refreshAccessToken still deletes the credential and throws when the local refresh token is missing or refresh_expires_date has passed, and that check runs before refreshOAuthTokens. With credential sync enabled, the parent app holds the real tokens and the local refresh token may be expired or absent, which is exactly when the sync endpoint should be called. Instead the row is deleted, the sync URL is never hit, and the user must reconnect Lark. The sync branch has to run before this destructive local-token check.

findings.title: No tests for credential sync or shared OAuth refresh
findings.body: This PR changes token refresh for Google, Office 365, Zoom, HubSpot, Lark, Webex, Zoho, and Salesforce and adds a webhook that writes credential rows, but it adds no tests. The PR checklist says tests were not added and were not run. The sync-disabled path needs a test that a provider response without refresh_token does not overwrite the stored refresh token and that credential.key is the token object, not a Zod safeParse wrapper. The sync-enabled path needs tests that the outbound request is authenticated, sends the user id rather than the credential id, and that each adapter can read the response. Without that, the credential corruption in parseRefreshTokenResponse and Google CalendarService is not caught before deploy.
